question: A 24-year-old man presents with a two-month history of a painless, hard, irregular swelling of the right testis. Ultrasound confirms an intratesticular mass. Which of the following best describes the correct diagnostic and surgical approach?

answers.text: Trans-scrotal biopsy of the mass, followed by orchidectomy if malignant

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Trans-scrotal biopsy is absolutely contraindicated — it disrupts the lymphatic drainage, altering the predictable para-aortic nodal spread to inguinal nodes and complicating staging and radiotherapy planning.

answers.text: Measure serum AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH; then perform radical inguinal orchidectomy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pre-operative tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) are mandatory for staging and monitoring. The diagnostic and therapeutic operation is radical inguinal orchidectomy with high ligation of the cord — never a scrotal approach.

answers.text: Start BEP chemotherapy empirically after ultrasound confirmation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chemotherapy without pathological diagnosis is inappropriate; the diagnosis and lymph-node staging must be established with radical inguinal orchidectomy and markers first.

answers.text: Arrange scrotal MRI before any surgery to characterise the mass

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI adds little over a high-quality scrotal ultrasound and should not delay orchidectomy; tumour markers and inguinal exploration are the priorities.

overallFeedback.feedback: Two absolute rules for suspected testicular cancer: (1) never biopsy trans-scrotally — it disrupts lymph drainage; (2) always send markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) before surgery. The operation is radical inguinal orchidectomy.
Correct. Intratesticular mass in a young man: markers (AFP/beta-hCG/LDH) + radical inguinal orchidectomy. Never a scrotal biopsy or scrotal incision.
